subject: microbiology
title: Virus Structure, Capsid Symmetry, Envelope, Replication and Inclusion Bodies

steps.tx: A **virion** is a nucleic acid genome protected by a protein **capsid**, sometimes surrounded by a lipid envelope bearing viral glycoprotein spikes. Genomes may be DNA or RNA, single or double stranded, linear or circular, segmented or nonsegmented. Viruses lack ribosomes and independent energy production, so replication requires a living host cell. Structure predicts environmental stability and disinfectant susceptibility.
steps.say: Genome plus capsid defines the virion; an envelope adds entry tools but also fragility.

left.title: Core components
points: DNA or RNA genome, never both in one virion
Capsid protects genome and aids delivery
Some virions carry polymerases or enzymes
No protein synthesis machinery of their own

right.title: Envelope components
points: Host derived lipid bilayer
Viral spikes mediate attachment and fusion
Matrix proteins may line the membrane
Detergents and drying inactivate many enveloped viruses

steps.tx: **Capsid symmetry** is commonly helical, icosahedral or complex. Helical nucleocapsids form flexible rods in many RNA viruses; icosahedral capsids package genomes efficiently in DNA and RNA viruses; poxviruses have complex brick-shaped architecture. Capsid proteins can self assemble around the genome, and symmetry seen by electron microscopy historically helped classify viruses before genome sequencing became the standard taxonomic language.
steps.say: Helical, icosahedral and complex symmetry are the three classic capsid architectures.

left.title: Helical
points: Protein units spiral around nucleic acid
Often enclosed in an envelope
Examples include influenza and measles nucleocapsids
Length can vary with genome

right.title: Icosahedral and complex
points: Twenty triangular faces enclose genome efficiently
Adenovirus has fibres at vertices
Poxviruses show complex internal structures
Bacteriophages combine head, tail and fibres

steps.tx: The viral **envelope** is acquired by budding through plasma, nuclear, Golgi or endoplasmic reticulum membranes depending on the virus. Enveloped viruses are generally more sensitive to desiccation and detergents than non enveloped viruses, which survive better on surfaces and in the gut. This distinction guides disinfectant choice and explains why norovirus and poliovirus persist environmentally while influenza and coronaviruses are easier to inactivate.
steps.say: Non enveloped viruses are environmentally tougher; enveloped viruses depend on an intact lipid coat.

left.title: Enveloped pattern
points: Budding acquires host membrane
Spikes are major neutralising antibody targets
Alcohol and detergent usually disrupt envelope
Examples: influenza, HIV, HBV and coronaviruses

right.title: Non enveloped pattern
points: Released often by cell lysis
Resistant to acid and many disinfectants
Faecal oral spread is common
Examples: poliovirus, norovirus, adenovirus and HAV

steps.tx: A generalised **viral replication cycle** proceeds through attachment, penetration, uncoating, genome replication and viral protein synthesis, assembly and release. DNA viruses commonly replicate in the nucleus, with poxvirus a cytoplasmic exception. Plus sense RNA can act directly as messenger RNA, whereas negative sense RNA viruses must carry RNA dependent RNA polymerase in the virion. Retroviruses reverse transcribe RNA into DNA.
steps.say: Attachment through release is one pathway, but genome type decides the molecular shortcuts.

steps.tx: **Cytopathic effect** is the visible injury produced in cultured cells: rounding, swelling, syncytium formation, detachment or lysis depending on the virus. It allows laboratories to suspect replication before identification by antigen, nucleic acid or neutralisation methods. Some viruses cause little cytopathic effect and need immunofluorescence or molecular assays. Cell culture phenotype remains useful for phenotyping and antiviral susceptibility in reference settings.
steps.say: Cytopathic effect is the culture footprint; its pattern hints at the virus family.

left.title: Patterns
points: Syncytia from cell fusion in RSV and measles
Rounding and detachment in many enteroviruses
Grape like clusters in adenovirus
Slow focal change in CMV

right.title: Uses
points: Initial recognition of viral growth
Quantification by plaque assay
Neutralisation tests measure antibody inhibition
Reference labs use it for unusual isolates

steps.tx: **Inclusion bodies** are intracellular accumulations of viral proteins or particles visible by light microscopy. Negri bodies are cytoplasmic inclusions in rabies infected neurons; Guarnieri bodies occur in poxvirus infection; Cowdry type A nuclear inclusions occur in herpesvirus infection; and CMV produces large owl eye nuclear inclusions. They are powerful morphology clues when present but lack sensitivity compared with PCR and immunohistochemistry.
steps.say: Inclusion bodies localise viral factories, from Negri bodies in rabies to owl eye CMV.

left.title: Cytoplasmic inclusions
points: Negri bodies in rabies neurons
Guarnieri bodies in poxvirus infection
Molluscum bodies in molluscum contagiosum
Rabies antigen testing is more sensitive than inclusion search

right.title: Nuclear inclusions
points: Cowdry A in HSV and VZV
Owl eye in CMV infected cells
Inclusions can overlap morphologically
Immunostains and PCR identify the agent
